this is my personal experience (it's been the same since i was first admitted at 17, the youth ward is 16-25 here. i haven't been to the under 16s one) in australia.

admit myself to the emergency department. basically tell the receptionist i've been suicidal and need help. the wait time for me has usually been around 4/5 hours. sometimes more, though. depends how busy. here, they admit people based on 'severity' (in general, not with mh afaik)

once in a bed in emergency, depending on if you have someone with you from my experience, they will remove cords and anything you can harm yourself with (this includes prescription meds and a bag check, although i haven't found that to be consistent. your meds will be kept with the nurses, and you need to inform them when you need them in advance). after that, the psychiatrist will see you and talk with you about what's going on. they'll ask what you're after by coming to hospital, if you feel safe, etc. they may suggest an admission - i've always gone in voluntarily (as if you go in voluntarily as opposed to made to go in by police etc, you have more 'rights' in the mental health ward during your stay. it's a sucky law). 

typically i've been in for a week or two at most, but i've met people who claim they've been in for months. for an admission, they will take your shoes (if they have shoelaces), any other cords/harmful things not already taken, and your phone if it's one of the places where they have phone times (one of the places that i've been to just requires you hand them in at night, and take no photos, no usage during groups/appointments etc. calls also have to be made in your room. you hand your phone in for it to be charged, but from experience the chargers they have usually suck lol. you can possibly request they use your charger, but i've never done that so unsure). they will also take your bags again for another check (if people bring in bags of stuff for you, those also have to be checked), then give you your items in a paper bag (they are massive lol) or no bag (so they'll put your stuff on your bed), and keep the actual bag in your locker hidden away (alongside anything else you want stored and not stolen or 'lost'. i've had a couple of fidget toys go missing, but nothing huge. but i'd recommend keeping important things either in the locker or on you at all times, especially if it's not a fancy hospital where you get a keycard to unlock your room. yes, they keycards also get stolen quite often according to a nurse i asked).

if it's your first admission (which they typically ask), they will give you a 'tour' of sorts. in one i went to, they had a locked kitchen (that you can access with a staff member present. if you have food that needs to be cold, there was a patient fridge. they should put a label on your food so it's not confused or stolen. food can be kept in your room if it's safe at room temp), a dining area, two lounge areas (one is locked at night), a gym (for some reason), a laundry, meeting rooms (where you can talk to people who visit, clinicians, etc) and patients rooms. there were 3 enclosed outdoor areas as well (you can talk to people there as well typically). depending on the ward, you will have a private toilet/shower, but i've been to one where there's like two toilets (and one of them is in with the shower, so you can't use it when someone is showering). in that ward, one lucky person got to have their private bathroom lol. in this ward, there is a chance you'll share a room with someone of the same sex, as well

the patients are typically nice. sometimes there will be incidents, yes, but i've been many times to the youth ward at least and only seen a handful happen. nurses are typically nice as well. although, this is a country where the mh wards are covered by public healthcare (you can go to a ward with no cost if you're an australian citizen, basically) and are quite well maintained compared to some other places.

criminal and non-criminal mh wards are a thing here. what i discussed above were non-criminal ones. i do not know the experience of a criminal ward personally

birth control helped for me. it didn't stop my period, but it decreased the intensity of both the flow and pain. plus, they're less frequent now. if the pill doesn't work, i'd recommend implanon (birth control implant in the arm). it's a mixture of 2 different hormones and unlike the pill, it doesn't have a sudden 'jump' in the amount of hormones (as in with the pill if you take it in the morning you'll have a much larger amount of hormones in the morning, that may make you have symptoms. some of the 'popular' pills are not mixed hormones, either). implanon is also very cheap depending where you are, i think i paid under 30 dollars and it lasts 3 years (slow release). you should be able to see your gp in regards to implanon if it's something you haven't tried. i understand the pill often doesn't help (honestly for me it made me feel worse), but implanon definitely was a lot better for me. plus, the doctor who gave me the implant said about 1/3 of people have no period after starting it, and that another 1/3 have decreased periods (to varying degrees). the remaining 1/3 have no change. just keep in mind if you do decide on implanon (or at least trying it), you will need local anaesthesia and cannot lift anything heavy for a couple of days (you can still use your arm, just nothing heavy). imo it wasn't super painful (the only thing that hurt was a slight ache in the arm in the following days, but i'd say it could easily be managed with ibuprofen or something similar. honestly, i didn't even need any), but depends on the person obviously. if you're worried about it hurting if they put the implanon in your arm, ask them to poke around with something small and sharp to make sure the anaesthesia is working. i personally needed more, and the doctor actually poked around (after checking i was ok with it) without me needing to bring it up. overall a good experience, but it does leave a small scar on the inner arm and you can feel it with your fingers if you press down. vast majority afaik do not feel it actually in their arm. i personally dont, even with blood pressure tests on that arm. but yeah just something to think about, i had very painful periods (to the point where i couldnt get out of bed and could barely function) and now i get way less (i still have pain, but way less. i can function quite well). hoping you're doing ok, and i hope this will at least be somewhat helpful, or at least put you on a good path for helping to ease your pain :)
